entry.summary: FlatMerkle: Logarithmic-Space Inclusion Proofs over a Single Linear Hash Stream IACR ePrint · Oct 14, 2026This paper presents FlatMerkle, a construction that gives Merkle-tree-style inclusion proofs with logarithmic size and verification time over an ordinary linear hash stream. It works by periodically writing the hash function's past internal states back into the data as ordinary content, so the final digest is a single unmodified hash call. The construction supports compact proofs for any element and proofs that a published file is malformed.

entry.title: Measuring On-Chain Cost of Output-Private Distributed VRFs on Ethereum
entry.summary: Unveiling the Cost: Gas-Efficient Output-Private Distributed VRFs on Ethereum IACR ePrint · Oct 15, 2026This paper compares two output-private distributed verifiable random functions, FlexiRand (pairing-based) and IcyVeil (pairing-free), by implementing both on the Ethereum Virtual Machine behind a shared coordinator contract. The pairing-free IcyVeil verifier uses about 57% less execution gas in isolation, and roughly 11% less across the full request lifecycle. However, its distributed evaluation requires about 2.5 to 8.2 times more aggregate committee compute, depending on the committee configuration.

entry.title: Tulva: A Practical Asynchronous Threshold FHE Scheme
entry.summary: Tulva: Practical Asynchronous Threshold FHE IACR ePrint · Oct 15, 2026Fully homomorphic encryption allows computation on encrypted data, but its single secret key is a single point of failure. This paper presents Tulva, which splits the key among K parties so that any t of them can decrypt, without needing to coordinate or be online at the same time. The scheme adds asynchronous threshold decryption to a base FHE scheme in a modular way, and the authors report 3.7 ms and 0.5 ms for partial decryption and share combination in a 16-out-of-512 setting.

entry.title: A scalable, robust threshold ECDSA signing protocol for many signers
entry.summary: Robust ECDSA Threshold Signing at Scale IACR ePrint · Oct 15, 2026This paper presents an efficient, scalable, and robust threshold ECDSA signing protocol for the case t≤(n-1)/3, for example for bridging consensus between blockchains. It allows pre-processing material to be computed in batches to speed up online signing. The authors combine established secret-sharing techniques with recent efficient zero-knowledge proofs. Experiments show the protocol is practical even with a large number of parties.

entry.title: Issuer-independent decentralized exchange for e-cash, letting users swap between two separately issued digital cash currencies without each issuer taking part.
entry.summary: Issuer-Independent Decentralized Exchange for E-Cash IACR ePrint · Oct 15, 2026The paper presents an e-cash exchange where a liquidity provider holds inventories of two independently issued currencies and users trade between them without either issuer joining individual swaps. It combines a blockchain settlement layer that automates and publicly verifies execution with an exchange-compatible e-cash protocol. The authors formalize new privacy requirements and build a compact realization with publicly verifiable payments and aggregate anonymous reissue, and prove its security and privacy properties under stated assumptions.

entry.title: Aerie: A proof system that aggregates post-quantum Falcon signatures into one short proof
entry.summary: Aerie: Efficient Aggregation of Falcon Signatures IACR ePrint · Oct 16, 2026This paper presents Aerie, a proof system that aggregates Falcon-512 and Falcon-1024 signatures, the post-quantum signatures selected by NIST, into a single short proof. Aerie keeps each signature's short random salt in the aggregate, so the verifier computes hashes directly and the proof covers only algebraic and norm checks. On an Apple M4 Max laptop without GPU acceleration, it aggregates 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures in 0.65 seconds, and verification takes 54 milliseconds on one core. The authors prove knowledge soundness in the random-oracle model. ★★★★ Notable: Aggregates Falcon signatures with a lattice SNARK, keeping salts so verifiers hash directly and proving byte-format rules; the authors report 0.65 s proving and 54 ms verification for 32,768 signature

entry.title: Weekend Crypto Volatility and Monday Risk: Whether weekend crypto price swings predict Monday variance in traditional markets.
entry.summary: Weekend Crypto Volatility and Monday Market Risk arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper studies whether volatility in cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin, Ether and XRP, which trade through the weekend, predicts Monday variance in the S&P 500, gold and a US Treasury ETF. The authors add a common weekend crypto factor to heterogeneous autoregressive models using daily data from 2017 to 2026. Predictive content is significant after 2024 and reduces out-of-sample losses, though statistical evidence varies across markets.

entry.title: Regime-aware multi-asset portfolio allocation using hidden Markov models and nested clustered optimization, tested on Indonesian assets.
entry.summary: Market Regime-Based Multi-Asset Portfolio Optimization Using Nested Clustered Optimization for Tactical Asset Allocation arXiv · Oct 20, 2026The paper proposes a tactical asset allocation framework that combines Gaussian Hidden Markov Model regime detection with Nested Clustered Optimization, with regimes identified out of sample. It is tested on an Indonesian multi-asset universe including government bonds, LQ45 equities, gold, CNY/IDR exchange rates, and Bitcoin over 56 out-of-sample months from 2021 to 2025. The regime-aware version limits maximum drawdown to 4.44%, but the regime-agnostic NCO shows a lower drawdown of 2.19% and higher cumulative return. The authors find that a rolling 24-month HMM switches regimes in 55 of 56 months, causing regime drift that erodes the expected gains.

entry.title: Fuji: How Demand Bursts Take Shape, What They Consist Of, and How They Spread on Robinhood Chain
entry.summary: Fuji: The Shape, Composition, and Spread of Demand Bursts on Robinhood Chain arXiv · Oct 27, 2026This paper measures sudden surges in demand on a blockchain marketplace, using Robinhood Chain, a layer-2 network, over its first three active months and more than 50 million Uniswap swaps. During bursts, traders touch about as many pools as in quiet periods, mostly different ones, and trade more intensively, with median peaks 2.5 times normal load. The rise and fall of demand are described by two exponential functions, and the authors compare two explanations for bursts, finding externally triggered cascades fit the data better than self-excitation.

entry.title: Performance guarantees for a permissionless lending protocol
entry.summary: Performance Guarantees for Permissionless Lending arXiv · Oct 26, 2026This paper proposes a lending protocol that the authors say carries far fewer risks than pool-based protocols such as Aave and Compound. Lenders and borrowers make competing interest-rate offers, and loans carry a fixed rate for their full term. The authors model collateral value as a random walk and use characteristic functions and Fourier inversion to derive exact expressions for liquidation and repayment-shortfall probabilities, illustrated with Bitcoin collateral.

entry.title: Decentralized medical data sharing system using off-chain storage and view-based access control
entry.summary: Decentralized Medical Data Sharing with Off-chain Storage and View-based Access Control arXiv · Oct 25, 2026This paper proposes VASCO, a decentralized medical data sharing system that does not rely on a central server, a specific cloud storage such as IPFS, or a secure channel. It encrypts both data and metadata end-to-end, using eight chaincodes built on view-based access control. The authors report scalability tests on a 21-peer blockchain and interoperability checks across 30 combinations of standards, formats, and protocols.

entry.title: BE-CTDE: Blockchain-based multi-agent learning with anomaly detection and token incentives
entry.summary: BE-CTDE: Blockchain-Enabled Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Anomaly Detection and Token Economics arXiv · Oct 25, 2026This paper proposes BE-CTDE, a framework that uses blockchain as a training-management layer for multi-agent reinforcement learning. A behavioral verifier compares executed trajectories with shared-policy recommendations, and token mechanisms (slashing, burning, rewards, compensation) adjust each agent's influence on the global policy update. In multi-agent path finding experiments, it achieves higher success rates under attack, even when adversaries are a majority, with collision rates up to 35% lower than detection without economic consequences and up to 43% lower than conventional stake slashing.

entry.title: Temporal liquidity matching for blockchains: an EIP-1559 extension admitting transactions below the base fee
entry.summary: Temporal Liquidity Crossing for Blockchains: An EIP-1559 Extension for Admission Below the Base Fee arXiv · Oct 22, 2026The paper proposes temporal liquidity markets (TLM), in which transactions seeking early block execution (consumers) fund transactions that accept later execution (providers). In a block-local EIP-1559 extension, providers can be admitted below the base-fee floor, and their gas is excluded from the ordinary demand controller input. The authors state an adversary model with strategic senders and builders and prove eight properties, including validator-checked rule validity, full burning of the base fee, and no subsidy.

entry.title: Cambium: Shared Commitment Roots Built by Participants
entry.summary: Cambium: Participant-Built Commitment Roots for Shared Digital Infrastructure arXiv · Oct 22, 2026This paper presents Cambium, a permissioned peer-to-peer service in which participants jointly build each cycle's commitment root, so no single party decides which inputs it includes. Fixed-size committees certify inputs, and a recursive-doubling merge spreads root construction across all nodes. A Go prototype on AWS completed cycles in 12 to 148 ms, verified proofs in under 1.5 ms, and showed logarithmic growth.

entry.title: Who Patches the Lightning Network? Release-line analysis of Lightning gossip, 2023–2026
entry.summary: Who Patches the Lightning Network? Evidence from Release Lines in Gossip, 2023-2026 arXiv · Oct 22, 2026The paper infers which software release line each Lightning node runs by matching the feature bits it announces in public gossip against implementation sources. Analyzing 814 daily graph snapshots from 2023 to 2026, it finds nodes upgrade on release and platform schedules rather than after security disclosures. The authors suggest that platforms packaging releases are the main lever for nodes that lag behind. ★★★★★ Notable: The authors infer node release lines from Lightning gossip feature bits and, across 814 daily snapshots, report that platform packaging drives patching more than vulnerability disclosures.

entry.title: Why Ethereum-style SDK defaults fail on UTXO-style chains: three reusable design patterns
entry.summary: When EVM Defaults Break: Three SDK Patterns for UTXO-Family Wallets arXiv · Oct 20, 2026This paper argues that mainstream Web3 SDKs such as ethers.js and viem assume an account-based ledger, a single secp256k1 signer, and transactions built without input selection. These assumptions break on UTXO-family chains like Nervos CKB's Cell model and when wallets use different cryptographic primitives. Using the TypeScript SDK CCC, the authors extract three recurring patterns from its release history and exported APIs: a declarative transaction composer, a unified signer abstraction, and a drop-in connector UI component. The paper presents these as transferable design lessons for SDKs serving UTXO-family ledgers and heterogeneous wallets.

entry.title: Using time-series foundation models to detect financial crime
entry.summary: Leveraging Time-Series Foundation Models for Financial Crime Detection arXiv · Oct 21, 2026This paper proposes TCEE, a framework that summarizes each account's transaction history with a frozen time-series foundation model and adds the relevant temporal context to each transaction's representation. These representations can be used for edge classification or as edge features in a graph neural network. Across six AMLWorld datasets, TCEE improves PR-AUC by 10.8% on average over the strongest baseline on five datasets and trains 6.0 times faster end-to-end.

entry.title: How Not to Be Censored: Guaranteeing Client Transaction Inclusion in Blockchain Consensus
entry.summary: How Not to Be Censored: Inclusion Safety in Client-Led Consensus arXiv · Oct 21, 2026This paper observes that blockchain consensus is typically client-server, with clients only submitting transactions and relying on validators to include them. The authors propose a leaderless consensus protocol in which clients actively participate and define inclusion safety, a guarantee that a client's transaction enters some block produced in an epoch. The analysis covers synchrony and asynchrony, showing that client or replica connectivity can substitute for one another, though relying on replica connectivity requires a longer epoch.

entry.title: PQ-Vault: A provably quantum-safe way to hold Ethereum assets without changing Ethereum
entry.summary: PQ-Vault: Provably Quantum-Safe Asset Custody for Unmodified Ethereum arXiv · Oct 21, 2026The paper warns that a quantum computer could recover the private key of any Ethereum account whose public key is already on chain. The authors prove that sidechains or bridges cannot protect such accounts without changing Ethereum's rules, so funds must move into a vault contract released only through quantum-safe primitives. They present PQ-Vault, combining this vault, a quantum-safe proof-of-stake sidechain, and an optimistic dispute protocol. ★★★★ Notable: The authors prove that unmodified Ethereum requires moving vulnerable funds into a vault released only by quantum-safe primitives, and show a quantum attack dropping compact certificates from 128 to a

entry.title: A blockchain consensus method where miners run AI inference instead of hash puzzles
entry.summary: Proof-of-Machine-Learning-Inference: Mining Knowledge, Not Hashes arXiv · Oct 20, 2026This paper proposes Proof-of-ML-Inference (PoML), a consensus protocol in which miners perform user-requested machine-learning inference instead of computing hash puzzles. The authors formalize the computational assumptions needed for ML inference to replace hash work and argue that LLMs and diffusion models satisfy them. They analyse security by reducing it to the Bitcoin Backbone model and evaluate block-time stability in a simulated environment.

entry.title: Fortress: A Fork-Resistant Transparency Log Using Social Graph Structure
entry.summary: Fortress: Fork Resistant Transparency logs Relying on Social graph Structure arXiv · Oct 19, 2026Transparency systems such as Key Transparency rely on external anchors like bulletin boards, blockchains, or out-of-band gossip among auditors to ensure everyone sees the same directory. This paper proposes using the social graph formed by users themselves as a replacement, formalizing a primitive called sg-FORT and constructing the Fortress protocol. In honest runs, out-of-band interactions occur only when users reset their secrets, and security is proven under standard cryptographic assumptions. The authors present this as a feasibility result under simplifying assumptions such as synchronous epochs and always-online users.

entry.title: On Pearl Blockchain's Proof of Useful Work: Systematization and Flexibility
entry.summary: On Pearl Blockchain's Proof of Useful Work: Systematization and Flexibility arXiv · Oct 19, 2026This paper revisits the proof-of-useful-work (PoUW) scheme from the Pearl blockchain white paper. It offers a systematic sensitivity characterization as an alternative to the Jackpot policy, along with an efficient algorithm for verifying the sensitivity condition. Building on this, it proposes a more flexible PoUW scheme in which each miner independently chooses its noise magnitude to balance computational accuracy and mining efficiency.

entry.title: Post-quantum IoT blockchain for securing edge and physical AI agents in critical systems
entry.summary: Securing Edge & Physical AI: Post-Quantum IoT Blockchain for Mission-Critical Cyber-Physical Agents arXiv · Oct 25, 2026This paper addresses the risk that quantum computers could break public-key authentication used in distributed cyber-physical systems and edge AI. It introduces rotational secrecy, an architectural goal that limits key exposure through authenticated transitions between cryptographic epochs, and presents PARS, a mechanism for coordinating key establishment, rotation, and reconciliation among agents. It also describes PARS-ESL, an optional permissioned ledger that records only security state such as key epochs, membership, and revocation, not high-volume operational data. The authors conclude that ledger-assisted post-quantum key-epoch management is feasible for selected edge AI and CPS security-control workloads under stated assumptions.

entry.title: Peer-relative trust screening to resist label-flipping attacks in semi-decentralized federated learning
entry.summary: Peer-Relative Trust-Guided Update Screening for Robust Semi-Decentralized Federated Learning under Label-Flipping Attacks arXiv · Oct 19, 2026This paper proposes a peer-relative trust-based update screening method to make semi-decentralized federated learning more robust against label-flipping attacks. It combines a robust validation-utility score with direction- and norm-based update quality measures. In experiments with 50 MNIST clients and 20% persistent attackers, the method reached 98.37% accuracy under moderate heterogeneity, rejecting 95.82% of malicious updates, and 95.25% accuracy under severe heterogeneity, rejecting 88.55% of malicious updates.

entry.title: Isotaxis: Optimal Asynchronous Byzantine Consensus with Ordering Linearizability
entry.summary: Isotaxis: Optimal Asynchronous Byzantine Consensus with Ordering Linearizability IACR ePrint · Oct 26, 2026This paper presents Isotaxis, a state machine replication protocol with ordering linearizability, designed to resist adversaries who manipulate transaction order, such as in MEV attacks. Its communication complexity is O(nℓ+λn²), which is optimal when ℓ≥λn, and it is described as the first asynchronous protocol to achieve ordering linearizability. Experiments on up to 100 EC2 instances show it outperforms Pompē at all tested scales from 4 to 100 nodes. ★★★★ Notable: The authors present an asynchronous SMR with ordering linearizability, reporting optimal communication and Byzantine resilience, and outperforming Pompē in 4-to-100-node experiments.

entry.title: Quantum Cadence: a post-quantum consensus protocol for multiple concurrent proposers that avoids certificates
entry.summary: Quantum Cadence: Post-Quantum Consensus with Multiple Concurrent Proposers arXiv · Oct 24, 2026Most high-performance blockchains rely on quorum certificates built from aggregated signatures, which large-scale quantum computers could break, and no post-quantum scheme matches their size and aggregation speed. This paper presents Quantum Cadence, in which each validator counts quorums from the messages it has received, so no certificates are needed. Its fast path keeps the optimal latency of Chorus, and when that fails it falls back to Coda, a signature-free Byzantine agreement. In simulations with 200 validators, its latency is comparable to Chorus and it scales better as the number of proposers grows.

entry.title: Tracing Money Laundering Across DeFi, Bridges and Mixers on Ethereum
entry.summary: Tracing Money Laundering Across DeFi, Bridges, and Mixers on Ethereum arXiv · Oct 23, 2026This paper presents FPTracer, a framework for tracing illicit assets through Ethereum services such as DeFi protocols, cross-chain bridges and mixers. It recovers intra-transaction asset-flow paths using a Context-Aware Transfer Tree, classifies transactions with cross-chain intent, and analyzes post-mixer activity using upstream laundering evidence. Evaluated on 20 real-world cases, it achieves the highest recall for known laundering addresses and destinations and finds 30 previously unreported bridge uses.

entry.title: SILMARILS-MV: An Information-Theoretically Secure Multi-Verifier Signature Scheme for Permissioned Blockchains
entry.summary: SILMARILS-MV: Information-Theoretically Secure Multi-Verifier Signatures with Dealer-Free Key Issuance and Linear Aggregation for Permissioned Blockchains arXiv · Oct 23, 2026The paper proposes SILMARILS-MV, a multi-verifier signature scheme that remains secure against unbounded adversaries and needs no trusted dealer for key issuance. Signatures can be linearly aggregated, and the committee can sign threshold certificates of constant size. According to the authors' analysis and HotStuff prototype, it reduces authentication traffic and cryptographic CPU cost compared with ML-DSA-44.

entry.title: DLT Terms 100: A Blockchain Glossary Based on ISO 22739:2024
entry.summary: DLT Terms 100: a learner's glossary based on ISO 22739:2024 arXiv · Oct 22, 2026This paper proposes "DLT Terms 100," a glossary intended to improve understanding of blockchain, or distributed ledger technology (DLT). The authors note that gaps between business and technical terminology, and confusion from existing financial terms being reused, hinder comprehension. The glossary is based on ISO 22739:2024 and categorizes terms by how often they appear in representative domestic and international literature and by difficulty level.

entry.title: A systematic survey of optimization tools for Hydra multi-party channels
entry.summary: SoK: Optimization Tools for the Hydra Multiplayer Channel IACR ePrint · Oct 23, 2026This paper is a systematization of knowledge (SoK) survey on blockchain Layer-2 scaling. It reviews existing two-party payment channel protocols and the tools built on them, explaining their core ideas. It then identifies use cases that call for new protocols for Hydra's multi-party channels, lists open problems, and suggests existing tools that could address them or serve as starting points.

entry.title: Tritone: Pairwise Garbled Disputes for Bitcoin Groth16 Proof Checks
entry.summary: Tritone: Pairwise Garbled Disputes for Multi-Party Proof Verification on Bitcoin IACR ePrint · Oct 23, 2026This paper presents Tritone, a protocol that lets Bitcoin enforce the outcome of verifying a Groth16 proof without changing consensus rules. It extends the two-party BABE protocol to a fixed committee of N operators, and the locked funds stay secure while at least one operator is honest. The authors formally prove security against up to N-1 corrupted operators and implement the protocol in Rust. They report transaction sizes on Bitcoin mainnet and local storage measurements. ★★★★ Notable: Generalizes two-party BABE to N operators with a Lamport-adaptor binding gadget, enforcing Groth16 proof verification on Bitcoin without consensus changes and reporting on-chain transaction costs.
